Author: @cactuskid-dc
Content:
Long-time DC resident there.  I love this channel but I was very disappointed in this video, which presents an extremely one-sided perspective.  Here are just a few critiques: 

First, it is inexcusable that the video makes no attempt to explain *why* the Founding Fathers decided to set up a federal district.  They did not do so arbitrarily, but because of the dangers of having the federal government be dependent upon a host state.  This omission robs the viewer of important context and the opportunity to contemplate whether DC's peculiar position is better than the alternative.

Second and relatedly, the discussion of BLM plaza was particularly one-sided.  It is true that the removal of BLM plaza was an example of the federal government meddling in DC's affairs.  It is also true that DC's *installation* of BLM plaza (one block from the White House) in the first place was an example of DC using its physical proximity to try to influence or "send a message" to the federal government.  (I would say the same thing about DC's poor handling of the BLM riots.). This undue influence on the federal government was exactly the sort of thing the Founding Fathers were concerned about with a host state, and why they chose to create a federal district. 

Third, the video is needlessly partisan in portraying conservatives/Republicans as opponents of DC.  I understand that Trump is the current president and his recent actions related to the District represent a new escalation, but DC has recently butted heads with both parties.  For example, just two years ago a major crime bill enacted by the DC Council was disapproved by Congress with a Democratic Senate and signed into law by Joe Biden.  This example is way more relevant and timely than some decades-old action on abortion spending.  (Also, if you are going to look at DC through a partisan lens, then shouldn't you at least mention that DC residents are *wildly* to the left of virtually every other geography in the country?  Of course they butt heads with Republicans more.)

Fourth and more generally, DC residents are portrayed as just normie Americans who are randomly held hostage by the federal government.  But DC residents are not separate from the federal government -- a plurality of us are direct federal employees, and something like half of us work in government-adjacent fields (lobbying, government contracts, nonprofits receiving federal grants, law firms practicing before the government, etc.).  And relatedly, much can be written about how, if DC were granted statehood, it would not be a  remotely "normal" state -- for example, we have essentially no agriculture or manufacturing, no landfills, and no car dealership (just to name a few).  In short, the governance of DC isn't normal, but neither is the city or its residents. 

 The truth is that DC does not belong only to DC residents -- it belongs to all Americans, and its governance properly reflects that.  I feel incredibly privileged to live here and I have learned to love our peculiar arrangement, even if it is suboptimal at times.

Author: @_Patronus_
Content:
Really appreciated this video on all the sticking points in the complicated relationship between DC and the federal government. It serves as a good jumping off point on the many historical and incredibly current issues in that dynamic. As someone who has lived in the District for just over six years now and has done a lot of my own grappling with these issues, just a couple thoughts:

1. The DC Delegate situation is often a lot more complicated than made out in the media and than you portrayed it here. Practically, the only power not afforded to the Delegate is being the *deciding* vote on legislation on the House floor. Delegates (including those from other places like Puerto Rico, Guam, etc.) can: vote on the House floor notwithstanding that caveat; they can serve on committees and subcommittees and even as the most powerful member of their party (either Chair or Ranking Member) on that committee; they can sponsor and cosponsor legislation; and very often they are respected by leadership and included in conversations like any other full member of the House. The biggest issue at the moment with the DC Delegate is that she is ancient and very clearly not up to the task anymore, prompting primary challenges for 2026, most recently by well-known City Councilman Robert White.

2. I was thankful that you framed the DC Budget Fix as exactly what it was, likely a incredibly stupid error by some staffer on the Appropriations Committee when crafting the continuing resolution passed earlier this year. It has had real-world consequences unfortunately, but hopefully should be corrected soon with the new continuing resolution in the works as we speak (both the House and Senate versions would return DC to its FY2025 budget). I really doubt there's any appetite for a repeat of this and I assume the status quo of basically automatic approval will continue.

3. I will talk more about the crime portion in my next point but I just wanted to say the National Guard deployments to DC were (thankfully) really mundane. My opinion, as evinced by the MRAPs and Hummers set up on Columbus Circle, was that this was really a publicity stunt for the satisfaction of the yokels who think DC really is a "warzone." They were mostly milling about, picking up trash, and powerwashing, almost all of them really looked like they did not want to be here, overall just a lot of nothing for the few camera shots.

4. As for the crime portions, this is my main reason for supporting the status quo as it has been since home rule was enacted. The City Council has very often and very recently gotten out of control with some of the legislation they've pushed for (often to Mayor Bowser's chagrin and opposition), mostly centered around loosening punishments for some pretty serious crimes, which have been rejected on a bipartisan basis in Congress and both the Biden and Trump White House. While yes DC's OVERALL violent crime rates are at 30 year lows, the homicide rate is the highest it's been since 2012. On top of that, it's per capita violent crime rates are much higher than many of the country's similarly important cities like New York or Chicago. All this to say, while yes certainly DC's statistics are improving and are of course nowhere near the highs of the 90's, but for such an important city to be so unsafe compared many other cities of import is unacceptable. I don't agree that a full federal intervention was necessary (or probably even effective, for that we'll have to wait and see), but clearly some course correction was needed. If the City Council does not recognize that their 2021 experiments are not working, I hope that these interventions and the continued poor showing in crime statistics nationally will give them pause.

At the end of the day, while of course DC has a fantastic and culturally relevant local population, many of whom have lived here for generations, it is still the national capital. Americans (and international visitors) come from all over to lobby their government, to go to well-respected colleges, to work or intern, and even just to visit all of the renowned museums, monuments, and events that happen here. It should be held to a higher standard because of this importance and I would think there's widespread agreement on that. Obviously this conversation is ongoing and I welcome hearing from anyone that disagrees. Overall, great video Sam!

Author: @cheeseofmysteriousorigin
Content:
Lot of people in the comments (most of whom I assume do not live in or near DC) saying that DC should be returned to Maryland, just like what is now Arlington County was returned to Virginia.

First, this is *less* likely than DC statehood. Maryland's state government already gets criticism for the DC suburbs diverting state funds away from the rest of the state; for DC to become part of the state, it would almost certainly engender pushback both from the liberal residents of Baltimore and its suburbs *and* the conservative residents in the much more rural areas of the eastern shore and the panhandle. And it's likely that the issue cannot be forced on Maryland without its consent as the Constitution is currently written.

Second, DC residents do not want to become a part of Maryland. This would be unlike Virginia retrocession, which happened not even 60 years after DC's founding. Over two centuries of being legally independent from Maryland has given the city an identity separate and unique from Maryland. Washingtonians do not see themselves as Marylanders. They see themselves as Washingtonians. If the issue is forced on them, and they are told that they must become a part of Maryland, it doesn't solve the fundamental issue that the video describes: the people of Washington DC do not have the self-determination afforded to the residents of other states.

If people who live in DC want statehood, then they deserve statehood. You're welcome to argue about the feasibility, but any alternative to the status quo is *less* feasible than statehood, and the status quo, as shown, is untenable.

Author: @SouthernEli
Content:
Fun fact: When the compromise of 1790 placed the capital in Washington, DC, Maryland was still considered a Southern state. Southern leaders demanded a neutral capital district be established in the South before agreeing to assume the debts of Northern states, and DC was considered to be firmly within the South. 

Moreover,  the location of DC was considered not only part of the South, but it was intentionally adjacent to the home of the first president and its namesake: George Washington of Virginia, who was very much a Southerner and understood as such.

It wasn't really until the 20th century that Maryland and DC came to be increasingly associated with the Northeast and distinguished as an in-between "Mid-Atlantic" region, which term originally referred to the parts of the Northern states west and south of New England (NY, NJ & PA).

Had George Washington been from Hampton Roads, DC would probably have been along the Virginia-North Carolina border instead. Fun alternate history!

I'll be honest, I hate that we are still thinking of things in a "black vs white" way.  The dichotomy should be "racially diversive vs. unifying".  Both of these slogans can be thrown in the diversive bin.  Neither is wrong, but they both take us away from unification.  

When you start using tax money to paint these slogans on streets, it's clearly a dare.  "I dare you to change this".   This is why D.C. was wrong to do it. 

Does this mean the congressional conservatives are right to fight back?  Of course not.  Both sides need to find ways to work with each other.

Author: @davon1935
Content:
Oh no you dont.
Benjamin Banneker designed Washington D.C. after the original architect, Pierre Charles L'Enfant, left the project. Banneker used his knowledge of astronomy to make precise calculations for the survey and his exceptional memory is credited with helping to reconstruct the lost city plans, ensuring the project's continuation. His significant contributions as a free Black man in a foundational role helped to establish the capital and challenged prevailing racist ideas about Black intelligence. 
Banneker's Specific Contributions
Surveying the Federal Territory: Banneker was appointed to survey the land for the new capital and worked with Andrew Ellicott to establish the boundaries of the District of Columbia. 
Reconstructing the City Plans: When L'Enfant left and took the city plans with him, Banneker, with his photographic memory and astronomical skills, is credited with helping to reproduce the original design from memory. 
Placing Boundary Markers: His astronomical expertise allowed him to make the precise calculations needed to correctly place the boundary marker stones for the ten-mile square federal territory. 
Significance of Banneker's Role
Challenging Racial Stereotypes: As the first Black man to be appointed by the U.S. government to such a role, Banneker served as living proof against the theory of Black inferiority. 
Promoting Abolition: Banneker's powerful letters to Thomas Jefferson, challenging the hypocrisy of slavery, helped advance the abolitionist cause and was celebrated by prominent figures. 
A Legacy of Black Excellence: Banneker's work on the capital city is a testament to his scientific genius and his crucial role in early American history, leaving a legacy that continues to be recognized through public spaces like the Banneker Academic High School.
